title: We shipped our first AI-assisted game on Steam six weeks ago. It sold 13 copies. Here's everything we learned.
author: FoodTimely8137
selftext:
We're a small indie studio, two friends in France. Dark Dice Dungeon is our first game: a roguelite where you build your heroes' dice face by face instead of levelling up. It came out on Steam on October 9, after six months of work. We used AI tools all the way through, Claude for the code and the writing, other tools for the art and music, and it's disclosed on the store page.

Where it came from: I'm a huge fan of dice games, on the table as much as on screen. Too Many Bones is one of my favourite board games, and I've put hours into Slice & Dice. I love the moment you roll and have to make something out of the faces you get. What I kept wishing for was more story around it and more choices between fights: events, paths, decisions that change your run. So that's what we set out to build. Keep the dice rolling I loved, give it a narrative layer and more choices, and build the combat around what I love in Too Many Bones rather than copying Slice & Dice.

In practice, that means two things. Upgrading your dice faces goes much further than in Slice & Dice, with a lot more face effects to build around. And there are two adventures that play completely differently: in one, Lantern points are a resource you spend during fights; in the other, it's Rage. Each one comes with its own original dice face effects, for the heroes and for the monsters.

The numbers, straight from Steamworks:

\- 13 copies sold, plus 3 keys activated, 1 refund

\- $78 gross, $62 net

\- 135 wishlists added, 107 still open

\- 19 players, median playtime 48 minutes

\- 27 real demo downloads (the "free licenses" figure is far higher, but that's mostly people collecting free demos)

\- 1 player review, 2 curator reviews showing on the store page

We didn't sit still. Fifteen short videos, posts here and on X, a free demo, 65 copies offered to Steam curators. None of it was wasted. All of it came too late: our first wishlist arrived 16 days before launch.

About 5% of wishlists turned into sales, which is roughly normal. The game convinced the people who saw it. Too few people saw it.

What AI changed, honestly: it made the building fast. Six months for a game with four languages, PC, iOS and Android. That speed is exactly what hid the problem. We were always one more feature away from "ready", and nobody outside knew the game existed.

What we do differently now:

\- The page for our next game, Wildball League, went up four months before release, with a demo planned for Next Fest.

\- We work with several separate Claude conversations, one per job (each game, marketing, Discord, Reddit), that pass work to each other through shared text files. Nothing goes public until one of us has read it.

\- Translation got cheap enough to just do it: Dark Dice Dungeon has been in Simplified Chinese since Wednesday, with no native review yet. We'll see if that was a mistake.

Two questions for people here who've shipped:

\- When did you start collecting wishlists, and what actually moved the number?

\- Has disclosing AI on your store page cost you anything you could measure?

Store page, with a free demo (50% off in the Steam Winter Sale from December 17):

https://store.steampowered.com/app/5248650/?utm\_source=reddit&utm\_medium=post&utm\_campaign=aigamedev\_devlog\_ddd

comments.author: Ravesoull
comments.body: Your game just looks bad. No wrong wishlist farming and AI closure/disclosure can fix this.

replies.author: FoodTimely8137
replies.body: Fair enough. What looks bad to you, specifically? I was going for the same kind of look as Slice & Dice.

replies.author: Ravesoull
replies.body:
Ok, let's me explain 

1. The design is completely confusing. There are eight character cards on one of the screenshots. How are you supposed to tell who’s who from a screenshot? Is this a battle screen? A character-selection screen? What is it? Are the enemies at the bottom or the top? Looking at the boss screen, now I can see they’re at the top. In games, the player’s interface is almost always at the bottom, so the action typically moves from bottom to top, left to right, or in any direction in 3D. But in your screenshots, it looks as if your party is at the top. That’s because you gave your party red borders (why??), even though red is usually used to mark enemies. It’s unintuitive for the player.

2. Why is there a ton of text on the sides? What’s it doing there? Is it explaining the abilities? If so, why aren’t those explanations in tooltips? It all looks like Minecraft chat on the sides of the screen. 

3. Also, you generated a capsule with a lock on it. First, pixelated art on capsules doesn't work good. There are some exceptions like Slotbound, but if you look on To The Moon and Celeste, then you can see they use different hand-made arts, because they are more attractive for a players. And the next thing. Where is the location from your capsule in the screenshots? Dark castle, cool, but after opening game page I see square Excel madness, instead of the dark and dungeons. There is only a tiny little thing in the middle, like a placeholder. Why does all the action take place against such a tiny background? At least in Slice & Dice, there’s a top-down view, so you get a sense of moving through a world. Your screenshots don’t give you that. 

4. The overall design. Why are there frames around the characters? Why not arrange them together side by side, like in Darkest Dungeon? Why put red frames around the enemies to show that they’re enemies? That’s exactly the problem with your design, if you positioned the enemies properly, you wouldn’t need those frames. The frames also make the whole thing look very obviously vibecoded. Sure, you may have used Slice & Dice as a reference, but it’s a bad example, its frames are ugly too, and you’ve layered them on top of the general vibecoding look, e.g. lots of outlines, lots of separate elements each in their own rectangle, and gradients that are uncharacteristic of pixelart and beloved by AI image generators.

5. Animations, animations, animations. Why couldn’t you at least show a trail from one unit to another when an attack happens? One character jerks, then another jerks, and the player is supposed to figure out whose attack it was and where it landed. Just because you’ve seen something like this in Slice & Dice doesn’t mean you should copy it. Games need movement and life, not just triggers that indicate something happened.

replies.author: FoodTimely8137
replies.body: Thanks, this is the most concrete feedback I got. The capsule not matching the screenshots, the tiny play area and the missing attack trail are three things I can actually fix. Noted on the frames too.

comments.author: Famous_Ad_5611
comments.body:
Ok... I'm not an expert here so do keep in mind that I might be actually wrong.

1. Your game looks AI - I'm not saying it looks like ai-slop. It just looks AI. There's something about the overall aesthetic that immediately gives that impression. That doesn't necessarily make it bad, I'm just saying it looks that way. Do what you wan't with this information.

2. Can you explain your game to me in two sentences? Dude, I  read the short description, watched the trailer, and you know what? I still don't understand what the game is actually about.

All I know is that I don't level up and I... throw dice, and the dice level up? But why am I throwing them? What are my heroes supposed to do? What's the actual goal here?

You describe the mechanics, you show the mechanics, but WHAT IS THE GAME ABOUT?! TELL ME!

Sorry, got a bit too invested there xD

3. Those are still some nice numbers you've got there. Like srsly - you're actually selling copies, which is something worth acknowledging, especially in this day and age, with a game that has a very AI-ish look.

But if you think this is going to make you more than $200 without some serious marketing effort, I'm actually sorry to break the news to you...

comments.author: Kooker321
comments.body:
I like the idea of dice games a lot, but your game looks like spreadsheets (check out the logs on the left and right) and the middle is just AI generated art in boxes. The logs on the left and right should look like dice faces rather than walls of text. 

There are games in similar genres I've enjoyed, but you should play other strategy games to see how they make their game look more approachable and exciting without sacrificing tactics.

replies.author: FoodTimely8137
replies.body: Those side panels aren't logs, they're the stat sheets of your heroes and the monsters. But if they read as walls of text, that's on me. Slice & Dice has a similar layout, what do they do better in your eyes?

comments.author: TylerDurden1985
comments.body:
You're focusing on the wrong questions my dude.

This screams "it's a game".  What I mean by that is, "it's a game, it checks all the boxes of what a game should do to be considered a game.  It has gameplay that may scratch a certain itch for that type of interaction and dopamine hit".  It's not an exciting novel experience, it doesn't have high production value, basically there's nothing at all separating it from the millions of other "it's a game"s out there.

"It's a game" like that painting of mountains your grandma made with Bob Ross in the 80's was "a painting".  It's a scene, it's recognizable.  It may even look "good".  It's not going to be something people are clamouring to purchase though.

Also I have no idea what your game is about even after watching the trailer.  Your description starts off by telling us what we're not doing but never really explains what we are doing or why we're doing it. 

It's certainly A trailer and A description.  If I'm flipping through games in a discovery queue, this is one of those that I would most likely space out on over a period of 3-5 seconds and then click past before even processing anything I saw.  It doesn't capture my attention, even after forcing myself to watch the trailer in full.

That's not to say it isn't fun, it very well may be.  But if it is, nothing here is really convincing of that.  Every aspect feels like "bare minimum" necessary.  Animations are "there".  They're not exciting.  The dice, the focal point of your game, aren't very interesting.  The characters all look like generic archetypes, most likely because they're all AI without any real art direction.  AI isn't the problem, it's that you started and ended with "can AI make this image look like what it should represent" and there's no real thought or effort put into making it look interesting, with any style consistency..."It's a character".

If you want to make and sell PC games, you're going to want to look a lot less at "checking the boxes" for a functional game and more into "what story do I want to tell", "what can I offer gamers that other games do not", "do I have ideas for something novel or is this a derivative work" and if it's the latter "does this do something new, different, or better than the source material".  

Then when you're desigining it, you need more thought put into the style, animation, and UX.  AI can't do that for it and it likely never will.  AI doesn't have motivations or feelings.  It doesn't know what "exciting" is beyond a the tokenized characters making up the definition of it.  It doesn't know your characters outside of the generic aggregate of archetypes it scraped off the internet.  Those subjective  elements are what separate "It's a game" from "This is something I really want to experience"

replies.author: FoodTimely8137
replies.body: Best comment in the thread, thanks. "Starts by telling us what we're not doing" is exactly the flaw in my description, I'm rewriting it. And point taken on art direction: the next game starts from the story and the style, not from the checklist.
